result:
I want to write about the peculiar intimacy of strangers. There's something profound about sitting in a café, surrounded by people you'll never meet, yet sharing a moment with them. The woman in the corner arguing with her laptop. The old man methodically stirring his coffee, as if decoding something in the rotation. The teenager bouncing their leg, vibrating with some private urgency.

These people are more real to me than many of my "connections" on social media. I don't know their names, but I know the way the woman tucks her hair behind her ear when she's frustrated. I know the old man checks his watch precisely every seven minutes. I know the teenager's playlist is loud enough to leak from their headphones—something aggressive, drums like a heart that won't settle.

We are, all of us, mysteries in plain sight. The city is a museum of unlabeled exhibits. I find this comforting rather than lonely. It means my own unspoken worries, my own small rituals, are part of something larger. Someone might be watching me right now, wondering why I keep touching the scar on my left thumb, why I write in bursts then stare out the window for long minutes.

There's no conclusion here, no revelation. Just the ongoing fact of being alive among others who are also alive, each consciousness a closed room with the lights on, visible from the street, impossible to enter, beautiful for that very reason. The café closes in an hour. We'll scatter to our separate evenings. But for now, this strange togetherness holds.
